query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the Mo content in CoCrFeNiMox-Ni/MoS2-Ag-Cr2O3 composites up to x = 1 will reduce both the coefficient of friction and wear rate compared to the baseline Mo0.2 composition over a wide temperature range by promoting Mo-induced lattice distortion, σ-phase formation, and improved high-temperature tribofilm (oxide/molybdate glaze) formation.
generation.material_initial_state: Uniformly ball-milled powder mixtures containing 67.5 wt.% CoCrFeNiMox (with x = 0.2), 12.5 wt.% Ni-coated MoS2 composite powder, 15 wt.% Ag, and 5 wt.% Cr2O3 prepared by mixing at 150 r/min for 8 h before spark plasma sintering.
generation.intervention: Increase the Mo content in the high-entropy alloy matrix from x = 0.2 (baseline) to x = 1 in the CoCrFeNiMox-Ni/MoS2-Ag-Cr2O3 composites.
generation.conditions: Spark plasma sintering under vacuum at 40 MPa by heating to 1250 °C at 150 °C/min with a 3 min hold followed by furnace cooling; and ball-on-disk tribological testing in air using a 6 mm Si3N4 ball at temperatures ranging from room temperature to 800 °C under an 8 N load, 4 mm rotation radius, 0.15 m/s sliding speed, and 270 m sliding distance.
generation.structural_mediator: Increased Mo leads to intensified FCC lattice distortion and formation of a hard, Mo-rich tetragonal σ phase, while Ag, Ni/MoS2, and Cr2O3 remain at the matrix boundaries. At elevated temperatures, oxidation and tribochemical reactions yield a continuous, dense oxide/molybdate glaze containing species like Ag2MoO4 that provide additional lubrication.
generation.mechanism: The additional Mo impedes dislocation motion via solid-solution strengthening while the σ phase contributes to second-phase strengthening, suppressing plastic deformation and mitigating wear. At low temperatures, MoS2 provides a layered, low-shear lubricating film and soft Ag reduces adhesion, whereas at high temperatures the formation of a layered silver molybdate-based glaze further diminishes friction and material removal.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the Mo0.2 baseline alloy, the Mo1 composition is expected to exhibit higher hardness and a better overall wear resistance across all testing temperatures. Although the coefficient of friction may not be lower at every temperature (with potential variations at low-to-medium temperatures due to differences in tribofilm formation), a significant reduction in friction and wear is anticipated particularly at high temperatures (600–800 °C) where the dense glaze formation plays a dominant role.
generation.baseline: Mo0.2 composite, which is predominantly an FCC solid solution with minimal σ phase, exhibiting a hardness of 432 HV, friction coefficients of ~0.66 at room temperature (peaking to 0.75 at 200 °C and dropping to ~0.21 at 800 °C), and wear rates of 13.1 × 10^-6 mm³/N·m (room temperature), 98.1 × 10^-6 mm³/N·m (400 °C) and 6.6 × 10^-6 mm³/N·m (800 °C).
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable to self-lubricating high-entropy alloys processed via spark plasma sintering and evaluated under dry sliding conditions in air against Si3N4 ranging from room temperature to 800 °C under an 8 N load, 0.15 m/s sliding speed, and a 270 m sliding distance.
generation.uncertainty: While high-temperature performance improvements are well-supported by the formation of a continuous glaze and hardness gains from σ phase, the quantitative extent of friction reduction at low-to-medium temperatures remains less certain due to potential competing effects from thermal softening and variable tribofilm continuity.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare and test two sets of composites: one using the baseline Mo0.2 composition and the other using the increased Mo (Mo1) composition. Characterize both materials using XRD for lattice distortion and σ phase quantification, SEM/EDS for phase mapping and wear-track analysis, and perform Vickers hardness tests and compression tests. Conduct ball-on-disk tribological testing under identical conditions across a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C, then identify tribofilms via Raman spectroscopy after high-temperature testing.
measurements: XRD peak shifts and presence/amount of σ-phase peaks
SEM/EDS analysis of phase distribution and wear tracks
Wear-scar dimensions and calculated wear rates via profilometry
Raman spectroscopy of wear surface coatings, focusing on the presence of Ag2MoO4 and similar molybdate phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the Mo1 composite does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in wear resistance and if high-temperature tribological tests do not demonstrate a reduced coefficient of friction (or evidence of a continuous oxide/molybdate glaze) compared to the Mo0.2 baseline under the specified experimental conditions.
